title: How to document a post before reporting it
summary: Posts get deleted or edited once they are reported. Capture the evidence first, then report. One complete, well-documented report carries more weight than many quick ones.

steps.title: Save the exact link
steps.detail: Copy the post URL (it contains the post ID) and the account's profile URL. Note the handle and display name; the handle can change, the URL and ID do not.

steps.title: Capture the post as it appears
steps.detail: Take a full screenshot showing the post, the account, the date and time, and the engagement counts. Include the device clock or a visible timestamp.

steps.title: Archive an independent copy
steps.detail: Submit the URL to the Internet Archive's Wayback Machine (web.archive.org/save) or archive.today so a third party holds a copy with its own timestamp.

steps.title: Keep the original record
steps.detail: Where possible, keep the platform's own data for the post, not just the screenshot. Traced stores the native record and computes its SHA-256 hash, so the copy can be checked later.

steps.title: Record context and pattern
steps.detail: For harassment, list every post from the same account aimed at the same person, with times; volume over a short period shows a pile-on. For false claims, save the subject's own posts or credible reporting that shows the claim is false.

steps.title: Write down why it breaks a rule
steps.detail: Name the platform rule (e.g. X Hateful conduct) and quote the words that break it. Keep it factual.

steps.title: Don't engage
steps.detail: Don't reply, quote or share the post; that spreads it further and can complicate the report.

steps.title: Keep a log
steps.detail: Record when you captured each item, when you reported it, the report reference and the outcome.

evidence_types.what: The post as published, verbatim, with its exact URL and post ID.
The account that posted it: handle, platform user ID, profile.
Screenshot, archive copy, and the original record with its collection time and hash.
The platform rule it breaks and why, in plain words.
For false claims: the subject's own posts or credible reporting that contradict them.
Views, likes, reposts and replies when captured.
Repeated posting at one target, or repeated violations by one account.
